_comment: Guided tour for the time-resolved anisotropy wizard. The UI is a declarative AutoForm *wizard* (anisotropy.view.json), so steps target the bound attributes of individual wizard steps; the tour follows the same order the wizard does. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: Two decays, one fit — not a ratio
steps.text:
Excite vertically, detect through a polariser: VV (parallel) and VH (perpendicular). Right after the pulse the excited molecules are photoselected along the excitation axis, so VV exceeds VH; as they rotate the two converge, and that convergence is the rotational correlation time.

ChiSurf does not fit r(t). It fits VV and VH themselves, linked, sharing one lifetime spectrum and one rotational spectrum — because forming the ratio first destroys the Poisson statistics the weighting depends on.

Six steps, in the order the wizard runs.

steps.title: Four files, and they must be the same measurement
steps.text:
An IRF and a decay for each polarisation. All four are read on the same time axis, and the fit assumes they were taken under the same conditions.

The one to watch: a timing shift between the VV and VH channels mimics a fast rotational component, because the early part of the decay is exactly where photoselection shows. If the two detectors have different cable lengths or different IRF positions, that difference arrives as physics.

steps.title: Background is unpolarised, and that is the problem
steps.text:
Background enters VV and VH equally, so it pulls their ratio toward 1 — toward zero anisotropy. And it does this most severely in the tail, exactly where slow rotation lives.

That is why this is a step of its own rather than a checkbox: pick a region that is genuinely dark, because a region containing signal subtracts signal. The IRFs are then background-subtracted and intensity-matched to each other.

steps.title: g scales every anisotropy you will report
steps.text:
g = S_VV/S_VH is the instrument's detection bias between the two polarisations — gratings and detectors are not polarisation-neutral. It multiplies I_VH throughout, so it scales r(t) as a whole: a 10 % error in g is roughly 10 % in every anisotropy, r₀ included.

Measure it — tail-matching on a fast-rotating dye, or horizontal excitation — rather than leaving it at 1.0.

l1 and l2 are the channel-mixing factors of a high-aperture objective: a large collection angle mixes the polarisations geometrically and compresses the measured anisotropy toward zero. Zero is the right value only on a low-NA setup; leaving them at zero on a high-NA one reports a smaller r₀ than the sample has.

steps.title: One lifetime spectrum, one rotation spectrum, shared
steps.text:
This is what makes it a global fit: both decays are described by the same components, and only the polarisation algebra differs between them.

Keep in mind what the rotation times can mean. ρ = ηV/kT, so a 30 kDa protein in water at 20 °C rotates in roughly 10 ns — and a rotation much slower than the fluorescence lifetime is invisible: the molecules have not turned appreciably before they stop emitting, and the fit returns it as a constant offset rather than a decay.

That is the honest limit of the method. The accessible window is set by the lifetime, and only a longer-lived probe widens it.

steps.title: Create the fit, then check r₀ first
steps.text:
This builds the linked VV/VH global fit and hands it to ChiSurf.

The first number to look at is r₀. It should be at or below the theoretical 0.4 for a collinear absorption and emission dipole. A fitted r₀ well above 0.4 is not a discovery — it is a g-factor or a background error, and everything else in the fit is then suspect.

Then: are l1/l2 right for the objective? Was the background region genuinely dark? Is the slow rotational component slower than the lifetime — in which case it is extrapolated rather than measured?

The ? button has the rest.
